CONDUCTING A DISCUSSION:
DISCUSSION LANGUAGE
Reading Skills Week 3.2

SUMMARY
• A discussion is an activity in which students talk about a topic that is provided by their
instructor, and they demonstrate their understanding of the topic by telling other students
what they think about that topic. Most discussion responses usually relate to a point of
view, such as agreement or disagreement, as well as reasons for that viewpoint, such as
advantages, disadvantages, or personal experiences.

OBJECTIVE
• To take part effectively in a discussion, you need to:
∙ Be able to say what you think.
∙ Listen to what other people think and respond to their ideas.
∙ NOTE: You must remember to not only state your opinion, but you should always explain the reasoning why you hold your
particular point of view once you have stated your opinion.

EXPRESS
YOUR
OPINIONS
There are many ways to express your opinions and to respond to
the opinions of others. These statements can be based upon
observations (what you see in situations), or your beliefs (what
you understand or think about situations). These methods are
defined as functions, and examples of these are provided below.

STATING WHAT YOU THINK
The first step in expressing your opinion is to declare your position on that topic.
Begin a statement to introduce your point of view with any of the following
phrases:
● I think ... ● I don't think ... As far as I'm concerned ...
● I believe that ... ● I don't believe that ... ● As far as I know ...
● In my opinion ... ● My view is that … ● If you want my honest opinion
...
● In my view ... For me, … ● Well, if you ask me ...

2. ELICITING/ASKING SOMEONE FOR AN OPINION
One way to engage with others in conversation or meaningful discussion is to ask questions,
usually about their point of view:
● What about you? / How about you? ● What's your opinion?
What do you think? ● What are your ideas?
What do you think about…..? ● How do you feel about…..?
Do you agree (or disagree)?? ● Would you like to say something?
● Yes, but what about ….? ● Is there anything you would like to add?
To bring someone into a conversation that they have otherwise been quiet in, try:
You have been quite quiet up till now, but what do you think?

3. DECLARING THAT YOU AGREE OR DISAGREE WITH ANOTHER PERSON’S
OPINION
• When reacting to another person, it is important to clearly declare your point
of view in relation to theirs.
• Build a statement based on any of the following phrases:
● I agree with you… ● I don't really agree with you…
I totally/fully/partly agree… I totally/fully/partly disagree that….
I believe ... I don't believe ...
● I'm convinced that you are correct... ● I'm convinced that you are wrong...
● You could be right… ● That can't be right….
That's right That's wrong
● I must admit that I agree with you... ● I must say that I disagree with you...
● Yes, absolutely. ● I wouldn't say that ...
● Exactly! ● I don't think so
● The way I see it ... I don’t see it like that…
● It seems to me that ... ● It doesn’t seem like that to me...
● I can get on board with that. ● I don’t think that is possible/practical

• It is also possible to form combination statements showing some degree of understanding before introducing an opposing
point of view:
• You're right up to a point, but …
• I can understand your point of view, but...
• When agreeing or disagreeing with the opinion of another person, it is possible to directly connect your opinion to theirs
using the following auxiliary verb-based phrases:
Agreeing with a
Positive statement:
Agreeing with a
negative statement
Disagreeing with a positive or
negative auxiliary verb:
So do I Neither do I I am…. 🡪 I am not
So am I Nor am I I didn’t…. 🡪 I did
So did I Neither did I I want to…. 🡪 I don’t (want to)..

4. ASKING FOR CLARIFICATION OR OPINIONS
When listening to the opinion or reasoning of others, it might be likely that you do not fully understand the opinion
or reasoning of the speaker. In these types of situations, there are ways to ask for clarification:
● What exactly do you mean? Can you explain that again please?
● What is it you are trying to say? ● Can you tell us a little more about …?
What did you mean by …?

5. HOW TO INTERRUPT POLITELY
• In a normal two-way conversation, it is polite to listen and allow each speaker to speak. However, at times there may be a
need to interrupt or stop the discussion in order to either present an objection, declare disagreement or to ask for
clarification. If interrupting others, do so politely:
● I'm sorry, but ...
● Sorry to interrupt, but ...
Can/May I add something?
[declare an objection or disagreement]
[request clarification]

6. REASONING:
Whatever your point of view, whether you agree or disagree, it is necessary to
explain how or why.
One of the main advantages of [topic] is…. One of the main disadvantages of [topic]
is….
[topic] can benefit people because…. [topic] can lead to problems for people
because….
I think this is true because… I think this is not true/untrue because…
Another reason for this is because…. can be used to either agree or disagree when adding
a second point

CLASSWORK (PRACTICE)
Select one of the statements below and identify your opinion, and how you would support it. Use the
questions below as a guideline to what your answers should include.
• Do you agree, or disagree?
• How strongly do you agree or disagree?
• What are some reasons why you agree or disagree?
• Do you have any ideas or counter-arguments?
1. Students in higher education should be required to learn a foreign language.
2. Having a university education is necessary for a person’s success in life.
3. Subjects related to computers are more important than other subjects.
4. A good education is less important than a good health.

TOOLS TO USE
Use the Discussion/Point of View Template to
help you form ideas about your opinion, how you
can support it, and how you might counter any
views that oppose your opinion. You may use the
internet for obtaining information about the topic
you have chosen. This template will also be
available to you when you do the actual
discussion.

FORM GROUPS AND HAVE
A TRIAL RUN
